items.abstract: <jats:p>The prevalence of Large Language Models has seen growth in recent years, and the impending concern for data privacy, especially in high-risk industries like medicine, consequently continues to rise. The use of privacy-preserving algorithms helps combat the infeasibility of desensitizing large training corpora that are required by these models; however, the impact that these algorithms have on novel models’ utility has not been determined. This research paper proposes a benchmark that demonstrates the performance degradation of medical LLMs when fine-tuning with decreasing privacy budgets (epsilon), corresponding to increasing privacy. Two natural language understanding tasks, Named Entity Recognition and Next Sentence Prediction, are included in the development of this benchmark. Out of the four models studied (BERT, BioBERT, Clinical BERT, and Clinical-BioBERT), the BERT model demonstrated the most drastic drop in performance when tested with low values of epsilon, whereas the medically fine-tuned models displayed more gradual degradation.<p></p></jats:p>
title: Benchmarking Differentially Private Transformer Based Medical LLMs

items.abstract: <jats:p>Decentralized finance protocols are frequently exploited, creating a demand for fast and reliable repair of vulnerable smart contracts and validation that reflects runtime security. Large language models are an emerging source of patches, yet many evaluations rely on manual checks or self-assessment, which cannot confirm whether attacker profit is actually prevented. We introduce an executable benchmark that replays verified real-world exploits against patched Solidity contracts under a resilient protocol that permits alternate attack paths and controlled state variation. Our framework compiles candidate patches, deploys them on a forked chain, and tests whether the exploit still yields profit. The benchmark covers six test cases drawn from reproducible incidents and is released as open-source. Among the nine evaluated models, GPT-5, GPT-4.1, and Claude Opus 4.1 performed the best, mitigating four of six test cases. Microsoft Phi-4 was the most reliable open-source model, mitigating two of six exploits and producing compilable patches for the remaining cases. No model mitigated the H2O case once resilient checks were enabled, while a simpler access control flaw, BTNFT, was often repaired with minimal edits. Grounding validation in executable exploit replay provides a precise and scalable method to measure whether proposed repairs harden contracts at runtime.</jats:p>
title: Repairing DeFi Vulnerabilities: Benchmarking LLMs with Executable Solidity Exploits
